speechtext:
Mr. G. W. McPHEE (Yorkton) presented the eighth report of the select standing committee on banking and commerce.
Mr. McPHEE moved that the report be concurred in.

Will the hon.
member explain what the report is about?

On the 23rd of May, as
acting chairman of the banking and commerce committee, I presented the eighth and ninth reports, which were concurred in, as will be seen by Hansard of May 23rd, but by some oversight as will be seen by reference to the votes and proceedings at page 385, the proper entry was not made on the scroll.
Motion agreed to.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Johnston in the chair.
Post Office-Outside Service-salaries and allowances, $18,632,694.40.
Mail service, including mail service by air, $17,267,060.
Miscellaneous, including $5,000 for the payment of compassionate allowances to employees injured while in the performance of their duties, or to the dependents of employees killed while on duty, such payments to be made only on the specific authority of the governor in council, $1,286,675.
Yukon Territory, $150,000.

Total, $37,336,369.40.

I explained last night the reasons why this bonus was being paid to Mr. R. Hill. I think that my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Stewart) was under a misapprehension because if I mistake not he understood that this was to be a yearly payment. Am I correct in that?
I had not asked that question, but I proposed to do so.

It is not a yearly payment, as I think I stated last night, but a lump sum payment which carries no further responsibility for future payments. The bonus was based on a valuation of the patent rights granted to the department. Those rights are generally valued by outside parties and a percentage ranging from 5 to 7 per cent of the value may be paid as a bonus for the right of the government to use machinery of that kind.
I wish to give a brief history of this matter and especially as to the employment of Mr. Hill. I think I led the committee a little astray last night as to the number of years he had been employed. My information is that Mr. Hill came to the Post Office Department around 1924 or 1925. He was formerly employed as an efficiency man with the Civil Service Commission, filling a position equal to that of chief investigator. When the time came for changing the railway and postal facilities in the city of Toronto, which made a complete change of the railway terminals as well as the new postal terminals, Mr. Hill was invited owing to his knowledge of such matters to become connected with the Post Office Department. It was necessary at that time to employ a person who had a good scientific knowledge not only of railway terminals but postal terminals, and it was then that Mr. Hill became connected with the department. His trip to the United States was in connection with railway as well as postal terminals. He was accompanied by the chief engineers of the railways interested and other officials, and his expenses were paid by the Post Office Department. Afterwards the knowledge secured from the investigation that he made in the United States was used in connection with both railway and postal terminals in Toronto.
May I add for the information of the committee that we have to-day at Toronto the largest and most up-to-date postal terminals in the whole world, and I speak with absolute knowledge of what I am saying. To Mr. Hill is due the credit for the installation of a system in Toronto which is equalled by no other place in the world. Up to 1927 or 1928 the United States had the best postal ter-
Supply-Post Office

minals in the world, Chicago and other places in the United States being looked upon as having superior facilities in that respect to any others in the world. I am glad to say that Toronto is now superior to these places, and the same system which has been adopted at the postal terminals in Toronto will be adopted also in Montreal. Montreal will be placed on a basis equal to that of Toronto. Throughout all this work Mr. Hill was the engineer or mechanical architect in connection with the laying out of these terminals. During that time he had perfected, or at least invented, machinery that was necessary in connection with the railway terminals and which could not be found in the United States. The machinery that we could have purchased in the United States would not have met the requirements at the larger postal terminals in the Dominion. Mr. Hill invented certain machinery which places Toronto on the basis I have referred to. He did not come to the postal department as a permanent employee because the salary attached to the classification by the commission did not warrant a man of his mechanical ability accepting a permanent position. Mr. Hill to-day is still a temporary employee of the department under certificates issued from time to time by the Civil Service Commission to continue him temporarily in the service as long as we need him. We will need him at least until the completion of the postal terminals in Montreal. Let me quote for my hon. friend's benefit section 17 of the Civil Service Act: In the absence of special authority of parliament no payment additional to the salary authorized by law shall be made to any deputy head, officer, clerk or employee permanently employed in the civil service in respect of any service rendered by him, whether in the discharge of Ms ordinary duties of office or of any other duties which may be imposed upon him, or which he may undertake or volunteer to discharge or otherwise perform.
It will be seen that it was not in violation of this section that Mr. Hill was granted a bonus. The bonus was granted, not for any additional services he had rendered but for the right of the department to use for all time to come the machinery which he had invented and patented both in the United States and Canada. This machinery, as I have said, is used in our postal terminals and other large offices.

Was not this man a full
time employee and were not his expenses fully paid by the department while he was working on this invention?
They were.
Then he was paid for his time while doing this work.

No, he was not employed
by the department at night. He never applied himself to developing his invention while he was on day work for the department.

How does the minister
know that?

From the records of the
office.
From hearsay?

The hon. gentleman has no right to say that. I also know it from personal contact with Mr. Hill, because I was with him at nights looking over the work he was planning out, and I was also with him when he installed the system that is now in operation in the smaller offices for the distribution of mail. So I have first hand knowledge of his work in that connection. If the hon. member for Leeds requires any further information I will endeavour to get it.

I want to thank the Postmaster General for the extensive explanation. However, he did not refer to the matter that I asked him especially about, namely, the particulars of the patents in respect of which this allowance is made. It appears to me perfectly clear that this is an atempt to do indirectly what legally cannot be done directly.
No such thing.

Here is a man employed by the Dominion who to all practical intents and purposes is a permanent employee. In the course of that employment and as a result of information which he obtained from inspection and examination of the machines in the department he gets a patent in some way. I am not going to question how he got it. Under ordinary circumstances if he were with a private corporation that patent, I submit, would belong to the corporation, and he would not be, entitled to any extra compensation. However, the minister has decided to give him this amount. I am glad to know that it is not for more than one year. While I think it is irregular .and contrary to the spirit of the act, that is all I desire to say about it.
I do not want to get into an argument-
I do not either, but I want to place that on record.

-but my hon. friend is dealing with rural mail routes, and he should distinguish between the rural mail route and the ordinary route, rural it is true, from office to office. Some of the routes mentioned by the hon. gentleman are round trips and are not what we call rural mail delivery routes, for there are only ten of those routes in the whole province of New Brunswick. I think he is referring also to the transportation from one office to another, and not to delivery along the line.
No, I am talking about rural routes proper.
Until the end of last year there were only ten rural routes in the province of New Brunswick.
There are seven rural free deliveries, and the average rate is away below $45 a month.
I never made the statement that the average rate was $45 a month.
There is a misunderstanding about it, then; as a matter of fact the rate is altogether too low.
My hon. friend may be quite correct.
However, I do not wish to get into discussion at this stage of the session.

I would like to call the attention of the minister to the condition which exists in mail deliveries to settlers in my constituency of Peace River. I suppose
it is difficult for anyone who has not been living in a new district to visualize what happens. I have no doubt however that some of the officials in the office of the minister have had communications regarding the need for post office service and mail routes in some of the new settlements.
What is the name of the district?

There are three or four of them in the Peace River district. In connection with those districts there may be twenty-five or fifty families living from twenty to thirty miles from a post office. One applicant received. the reply that it would be too expensive to supply mail routes for those localities. I will admit the roads are not paved highways, but it seems to me that when there are about fifty settlers living twenty-five miles from a post office there should be some sort, of mail service. I think they have the right to expect this country to undertake development in their districts.
Is that in the Peace River, North Vermilion section?
No, it is northwest of Fairview.

In the Peace River section we are considering a flying service, so that delivery may be made by air mail. Owing to the lack of roads required to reach these people the air mail is now under consideration, and I can assure my hon. friend everything within our power will be done to give service. In connection with the expenditures of this department during the last two years our object has been to give as much service as possible; I am not attempting to keep down expenditure where I find service is necessary for the welfare of the people. I can assure my hon. friend the matter will be investigated.
Supply-Post Office

Will the minister tell us if we have had the last word in regard to salaries of letter carriers? I understand there is to be a general reference to the Beatty commission in regard to all civil servants' salaries. The minister has stated that he will be willing to have the money recommended in order to make the increases. In that connection I wish to ask him if any amount has been set aside in the estimates for the projected increases in this branch.
No.
Then these men will have to wait until the report of that commission is received and this house takes action.

I may say that it is true that the question of the salaries of this class, as well as others, has been referred to the Beatty commission and if I am not mistaken the lower paid officials will receive particular consideration, and there will be the matter of fixing a minimum salary for them. There is nothing in the present estimates which enables us to pay them for this year's work, unless the commission in its report would recommend retroaotion to April 1st, 1930.
Does the minister propose to abandon his efforts in this particular matter?
I certainly do not; I shall make it a point to attend to the interests of these men and if it is at all possible I shall appear before the commission.

But that may be a matter of a year or so. I take the word of the minister that he is anxious to do something, and that he recognizes the justice of the claim made by the letter carriers. In fact he has actually stated that their requests should be acceded to. If the minister were able to convince the Civil Service Commission in regard to the necessities of this particular branch, would he now be able to provide the money?

Not at the present time, or through these estimates. It may be done by means of retroaction. The, putting into effect of recommendations by the Beatty commission would depend upon the policy of the government holding office at that time. So far as I personally am concerned, I shall certainly stand behind what I have already attempted to do for these men.
The minister is obliged to say that reference to the Beatty commission shuts off any possible action along other lines?
No.
What other action does the minister propose to take?

It does not out off action, but rather gives us more action, because the reference to the Beatty commission will be investigated and there will be a reference to the government. I feel fairly sure that from the expressions of opinion on both sides of the house in connection with this question the government will be disposed to do whatever is proper under the report of the Beatty commission.
The minister has misunderstood me. He proposes to take no further action in regard to increasing the salaries of letter carriers, pending the report of the Beatty commission?
That is correct.

With a view to making further progress, may I suggest that the Hill matter to which we were referring is included in the item with which we are now dealing, the $5,000 for the payment of compassionate allowances. I have no objection to the passing of this item.

There is a man by the name of Kirk with whom there has been some correspondence. He was arrested, tried and acquitted but he lost his job. In the meantime he has paid a considerable sum of money towards the superannuation fund, and he cannot get it back. He cannot receive superannuation because he is not in the service and, I suppose, never will be. Has the minister made any provision to deal with such cases as this?

My hon. friend drew my attention last year to the case of this man; I know he does not wish me at this time to go into the particulars of the case. Under the refund clause however this gentleman cannot receive a return of the amount of money which was coming to him. May I explain that this refund clause is under the control of the service, not of the government? The men pay 5 per cent into it; true, the government does add certain other percentages to the fund. We have to be very careful in the administration of a fund which belongs to the service, and I remember that last year I was asked the question whether I would recommend a compassionate allowance. In order to do that I would have to bring the matter before the treasury board and from the treasury board it would have to go to the council. I promised the hon. gentleman from Toronto South (Mr. Geary) that I would go into the matter, and when I did so I found that if we once opened the door we

Supply-Post Office
would have to open it to hundreds of men who knew when they entered the service what the consequences would be if for cause they should lose their positions. I discovered that if we opened up this case we would have to take the same action in connection with 'hundreds of other cases and in this way deplete the fund which the men should have to their credit. I refrained from recomending to the government the payment of a compassionate allowance, and that is how the matter stands at the present time.
In the courts they said the minister had no right to dismiss this man.

No, the courts did not find against the minister. If the hon. gentleman wishes to go into the details of that case and have them placed on Hansard we will do so, but I think for the sake of the individual himself that should not be done.
Item agreed to.

The next item
I would suggest is the amount of S925 to provide for a telegraphic news service for the Magdalen islands during the winter months.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall the resolution
carry?
No, Mr. Chairman ; do you realize that if you carry the resolution you carry the whole thing? We are going through these items and picking out the ones that are contentious.

I want to
ask the Postmaster General whether he has yet applied to his department the recommendations of order in council P.C. 670, requiring the eight-hour day?

In reply to the hon. gentleman I may say that there is no need of applying it at the present time, because we have had it in effect for many years in the postal department in the large city offices, the classified offices.

May I ask
what is the practice in regard to small city offices?

In the small city offices,
or commission offices, the salary of the postmaster is made up of pay and commission. He employs his own help.
And the eight-hour day does not apply?
The hon. gentleman should possess his soul in patience; I will give the information.
I can give the information just as well.

Perhaps I can give it a
little better.

I should
like to get the information from one or the other of you two gentlemen.

The postmaster has the
right to employ his own help, but the hours of the post office are regulated by the department, generally from about eight o'clock in the morning until eight o'clock at night. In cases where the office is open later than that overtime is allowed.

In other
words, do I understand that the ten hour and sometimes the twelve hour day applies to employees working in post offices under the postmasters in small city and town offices?

It may happen, and it may happen without our knowledge. It may also happen that the postmaster has divided off his staff, giving each so many hours during the period between eight o'clock in the morning and eight o'clock at night.

In the event of the attention of the minister being directed to the fact that post office employees-and I use that term to include those who are hired by the postmaster-are in many cases working ten and twelve hours a day, will he see that the postmaster does not continue that practice?
I will, so far as that order in council applies.

I am delighted to know that, because I was to direct the attention of the Postmaster General to the practice in the post office in the town, or rather city of Drumheller, which I am informed now is an incorporated city. In that city I am told that employees in the post office at present are working some twelve hours a day and that sanitary conditions are such that with the long work days this combination results in periodical breakdowns of many of the girls working there. One of these at least, known personally to my correspondent, has to receive medical attention from time to time, and her doctor's advice is that the frequent breakdowns are the result of the long day and the unsanitary conditions. Even though this order in council only recently has been passed I think it is a disgraceful state of affairs that this condition should be permitted to continue. Certainly the minister must have known that in many of these smaller town and
Supply-Post Office

city post offices the postmasters, either with or without the knowledge of the Postmaster General but certainly with the knowledge of his department, have been employing men and women for ten hours or more a day, and in this case as I have shown, twelve hours a day. I sincerely hope the minister will keep his word and undertake to see that this practice ceases and that the eight-hour day applies to the employees of this post office.

This is the first time my
attention has been directed to the Drumheller case.

No, it is
not; I mentioned the matter during the unemployment debate.

This is the first time my attention has been officially drawn to the Drumheller case with reference to complaints from the employees as to their hours of work. I know there is a demand for a new public building at Drumheller, but that is a matter for my colleague the Minister of Public Works to work out. However, I can assure my hon. friend that since the complaint now has been made openly in parliament it will be looked into and I will see what remedy can be applied.

I understand there was a
revision in the salaries of the country postmasters when we adopted penny postage.
Yes.
Would the Postmaster General say how these salaries compare to-day with the salaries formerly received when we had three cent postage?

I do not know to what
class of office the hon. gentleman refers. For instance, if it is a small country office, at that time the postmaster received $60 a year as a minimum. Since the penny postage came into effect that minimum has been raised to $100 a year.

I refer to the offices in the
next class above that.

In the offices of the next
class the salary of the postmasters are on a sounder basis. They receive a larger remuneration to-day, since the revision of the commissions, than was paid previous to the penny postage. Since we inaugurated the penny postage, in order to give more pay to these people we have put in a new system of commissions. We have come across several cases of apparent discrimination, but these have been honed out, if I can Use that term, as speedily as possible. In other cases where

complaints of that kind were made they were carefully and immediately looked into, and lately we have been in consultation with the executive officers of the postal association throughout Canada with a view to bettering their conditions in that respect across the whole Dominion. That applies to unclassified offices, if I can use that term, offices below the city office class.

Do I understand from the
Postmaster General that these salaries are higher to-day than they were previously.

Yes, the superintendent informs me that upward adjustments have been made in all these cases. There are some people who claim that their salaries are less, but my hon. friend must distinguish between salaries and allowances. In some cases the allowances are taken to mean addition to the salaries. For instance, rentals, night work and forwarding allowances would come in that class. In many instances these forwarding allowances will be reduced because the number of offices to which mail is forwarded will be diminished in number owing to the introduction of rural delivery routes. Overtime and night work will be reduced owing to changes in train conditions for the delivery of mail.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: While it is not considered to be part of the duty of the chairman, I would point out to the committee that there are some 200 items in the main estimates, and some 100 items in the supplementaries still to be passed.

Has the
minister any practical way by which he could provide that all postmasters would be compelled to recommend and accept the eight-hour day for employees which they in turn hire?

The department will go
fully into that question.
Is the minister prepared to insist that some practical means be adopted to apply the eight-hour day to all employees in the department?
The terms under which these things are regulated by order in council will be carried out.

Mr. Chairman,
I want to assure the committee that I desire to cooperate in getting these estimates through as soon as possible, but I would like to make a few statements regarding the air mail.

Supply-Post Office
service. The amount involved by this item is $1,912,000, an increase of $712,000 over the previous year.
One or two days might well be spent in the discussion of this interesting subject. I have had certain returns brought down, one of which contained 760 pages of recommendations, contracts and correspondence regarding this service. It is a most interesting file, and it, together with other information which the Postmaster General has disclosed, should receive very serious consideration. It is impossible at this late date to do justice to this matter. It am not opposed to the air mail service; in fact, I have no hesitation in saying that it is most desirable that this service should be provided in the outlying districts. However, in the thickly populated districts such as between Montreal and Toronto and Montreal and Ottawa, where two railway companies provide rapid service, I do not feel that this large expenditure is justified; the cost of the service is out of all proportion to the revenue derived. The rate fixed by order in council for air mail is 5 cents for the first ounce and 10 cents for the second, which would amount to 80 cents per pound, or, if it were all based on the higher rate, $1.60 per pound.

The hon. gentleman is in
error there; it would amount to $2.60 per pound.
The return shows that the rate is 5 cents for the first and 10 cents for the second ounce.

There are about 50 letters
to the pound.

There are only
16 ounces to the pound.

If the letter weighed only
one-quarter or one-half ounce, It would pay the 5 cent rate.

I was taking the rates given in the return; however, I will accept the postmaster's rate of $2.60 per pound. From the information which the Postmaster General has supplied I find that the service between Montreal and Toronto cost $97,420.80 for the year under consideration. The total mail carried weighed 7,724 pounds, and this works out at a rate of $12.61 per pound. I submit that that is extravagant and out of proportion to the service rendered. The service between Montreal and St. John, via Quebec and Moncton cost $14,246.05, to carry 1,118 pounds at a cost of $12.74 per pound. The service between Montreal and Detroit cost $13,071.85 to carry 18,401 pounds at a cost of $7.45 per pound.
In going through the files I find that most of these air mail contracts have been let without public advertisement. I think there is only one case in which that practice was carried out. This is in striking contrast with the manner in which the Postmaster General deals with rural mail routes. If mail is to be carried for ten or twelve miles, the contract is put up for tender. The lowest tenderer receives a contract which would involve an expenditure of $400 or $500. An air mail service contract involving an expenditure of hundreds of thousands of dollars is let without public advertisement or tender.
The hon. gentleman is not quite correct in that statement.

The Postmaster
General may make his statement after I am finished as I have no desire to enter into a controversy at the present time. Any one of these air mail contracts would be worthy of very careful study. For instance, a term is included in the contract requiring the contractor to report after each trip his revenue from passengers or other goods carried. I asked the Postmaster General what the revenue was from these different contractors and his reply is: "I have no information," although his contract with these carriers provides that on every trip they shall report the revenue in addition to carrying the mail.. That has not been enforced. In some cases this provision varies. With regard to carrying the-mail into the United States, there are certain services running between Montreal and Detroit and Toronto and Buffalo, and it is peculiar that the contract does not contain the provision that they are to report what they are carrying on those trips. These are all matters that would require a great deal of time to clean up, and I did desire to make a motion substantially reducing this vote and to explain in detail my reasons for so doing. I am satisfied, if I had an opportunity to do so, I could convince the committee that here has been waste; that there has been extravagance and that the public interest has not been safeguarded in connection with the air mail service. But that would take entirely too long, and I am not going to make that motion at this time.
It is too long already.

Well, I will continue a little longer. I am going to refer, just to satisfy the hon. gentleman who has spoken, to an editorial in the Moose Jaw Evening Times of Tuesday, March 4, 1930. I under-
2S74
Supply-Post Office

stand this paper is not unfriendly to the Postmaster General or to the government; in fact it is one of their supporters. I quote this editorial in part; it is long and I do not propose to read it all. In connection with one of these air mail services it states:
According to the present existing orders this will be the daily program. For some reason or other the powers thait be at Ottawa have decided that the northern air mail will be flown out of Regina. That it will cost the Canadian people at a minimum at least $12,000 a year extra, makes little difference, apparently, to the individuals who regulate these things. Regina's pride and hoggishness must be catered to. The politicians have so decreed. The Postmaster General and Hon. C. A. Dunning, Minister of Finance, may be able to explain why they are willing to throw away an extra $12,000 a year on flight mileage, but to the citizens of Moose Jaw it has no other meaning than "political pull" by Regina, regardless of the cost to the people.
No other view is taken in Moose Jaw of this wasteful extravagance than that the Regina politicians have brought undue and unfair pressure to bear on the Postmaster General to order that the pivotal point in the air service must be Regina, because such an order would mean that the Western Canada Airways would have to transfer their staff of mechanics and their terminus, now at Moose Jaw, to Regina.
In the intervening months until the Regina hangar has been built and the bog which surrounds it has been surfaced in some way to keep the heavy machines from becoming mired, the planes will be flown out of Moose Jaw. There will be weeks pass, when it will be absolutely impossible to land a three ton plane on the Regina field without its becoming mired. Then some time late in the summer the field will be surfaced, if plans are carried through. For two or three months, the Regina field will be safe, and then when the snow begins to fall and drift, hard-surfaced runways or not, it will be just as dangerous as it was the past six weeks.
Premier Mackenzie King surely cannot be countenancing this barefaced robbery of the public treasury by those who for political reasons of "bringing home the bacon" are flaunting all economic argument and the opinion of their technical advisers and the desires of the contractors' who are carrying the mail.
The discrimination which has been shown by the Postmaster General for political reasons in favour of Regina is most apparent. With the mail routed out of Regina, letters by air mail for Saskatoon, Battleford and Edmonton from Moose Jaw will be carried east forty miles and then back again over an equal distance over the route to Saskatoon. This duplication of flight mileage would be completely overcome, if the mail from Regina for Saskatoon, Battleford and Edmonton was carried through to Moose Jaw on the plane which arrives here at 12.10 midnight, and placed on board a plane for the northern cities at this point.
I could duplicate that with respect to other services. All I want to say, however, is that this matter must some time, sooner or later, be thoroughly investigated. In my opinion

it cannot be done this session in this committee, and the only course that I suggest is that next session this matter be brought before the public accounts committee and a searching investigation be conducted in connection with all these contracts.

I court the fullest investigation under oath in regard to this matter. As regards the article which the hon. gentleman has read from the press, it is in reference to a row between Regina and Moose Jaw as to where the plane should land. The Post Office Department has nothing whatever to do with the matter. There is absolutely no duplication for which we are paying. Our contract is clear and distinct. I hope when the elections are over and we come back to this side of the house, my hon. friend will be returned if for no other purpose than to institute this investigation. I court it.

Those are very
like words that the Postmaster General has thrown out on previous occasions, and the investigations, when they were finished, showed that he was not justified in making the challenge. We found him wanting. Civil service discharges and refusals were investigated and it was found that the Postmaster General was openly defying the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
We have discussed that before.
Well, we are prepared to discuss it again if the Postmaster General wants that.
Not necessarily now.
I have endeavoured to be reasonable and moderate in my presentation.

Yes, but my hon. friend
issued a challenge for an investigation and I accepted it.
But the trouble is that the hon. gentleman will not be in his present position then.
I will, and nobody else can refuse an investigation.

The hon. gentleman knows very well he will not be in a position to accept it. This is just an effort to get by. That, however, is the situation. As I say, I have not nearly exhausted this subject and when it is all investigated, the file I have under my hand will make a very interesting disclosure.

Item agreed to.

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay

Railways and Canals-chargeable to capital -Canadian Government Railways: To provide additional oar ferry, and facilities for car ferry service, between the mainland and Prince Edward Island (revote, $2,000,000), $2,500,000.

Who gets the subsidy for
that ferry?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
There is no subsidy. It
is a government car ferry.

There is a subsidized ferry running across there, and I thought this was it.
Mr. MACDONALD (Kings)):	When will
that ferry be in operation?

The contract has been let
for the car ferry, and it is to be completed in July, 1931. I expect that it will be in service immediately after that.

Item agreed to.
Hudson Bay railway and terminals: Construction and betterments, including E. B. Jost a-t $2,500, $5,900,000.
I think the minister should make a statement in regard to the conditions up there.

The question is a perfectly proper one; I had intended to do that. This vote is for the purpose of carrying on the work that has been going on during the past two years at Fort Churchill in the construction of terminal facilities, and to enable us to complete the ballasting on the Hudson Bay railway line from The Pas to Fort Churchill. The amount is divided approximately thus: 81,900.000 for railway purposes, and S3,5(X),000 for the terminals at Fort Churchill. The railway expenditure involves the building of section houses and some stations, but mainly it is for the ballasting of the line. The work at Fort Churchill is for the construction of the new grain elevator, for dredging and for building docks and also for bringing in a water supply to the town.
What are the prospects as to the first use of the line?

It is not intended to open the Hudson Bay railway for commercial traffic before the autumn of 1931. By that time the docking facilities will have been completed, the grain elevator will have been completed, and sufficient dredging done to let the sea-going vessels come into the dock. My deputy now advises me that the docking facilities will not quite be completed at that time.
Before the autumn of 1931?
Yes.
Unless it is fairly early in the autumn, it would not be of any use until 1932; is not that right?
The elevator is expected to be finished early in September, 1931, or before, with facilities for the shipment of grain. Dredging sufficient to allow the boats to get in will also have been done.
It was for this elevator that Carter, Halls and Aldinger got the contract the other day, was it not?
Yes.

I have suffered a great deal from misrepresentation by hon. gentlemen opposite in connection with the Hudson Bay railway, and the opportunity is now afforded to enaible me to make a statement, which I propose to do.
Frankly I do not think I have ever said a word anywhere about the hon. gentleman's position on the Hudson Bay railway. Someone else may have done so, but I have not.

It is very gratifying to hear the minister make that statement. I had not the minister in mind; I was using the word in the plural not the singular, but I am grateful to him for that statement.
Last year when this item was under consideration we were discussing expenditures by day's work for the completion of the railway to Port Nelson, and I was attacked that evening just at the close of the session. Telegrams were sent out that I was endeavouring to prevent the completion of the Hudson Bay railway. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Thorson) was very solicitous about the welfare of his party. I came into this house in 1011, having lived in western Canada for some few years prior to that-a very considerable number of years as life is measured. I had heard of the Hudson Bay railway from the day I went there. It was common knowledge that on one occasion some forty odd years ago a telegram was referred to in a public meeting to the effect that the rails were on the sea to construct this line to the bay. In 1911, I was privileged to move the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and on that occasion I took the trouble to state my position with respect to the Hudson Bay railway, and' although it may be rather late to do this I feel that I should present the matter as fairly as possible and indieabe that at that time I was most anxious that the road should be completed. Without reading from the pages of Hansard, I said that the policy of the party was that the road

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
should be completed at as early a date as possible. The contract which had been awarded for a .portion of the road had not been proceeded with very far at the time of the election in 1911. The late Hon. Frank Cochrane, as Minister oif Railways and Canals, took the matter actively in hand, construction was pushed forward, and strange as it may sound to this house, the railroad was completed within 92 miles of Port Nelson at the time the- Liberal government came into power in 1921, so that ten years ago next fall the railroad was completed to within almost 92 miles of the bay. During the war the railway fell into a state of disrepair, but no action was taken to remedy that until 1925 or 1926. In the meantime the minister will perhaps recall that while he was a member of the Union government the matter was under discussion, but it was felt that conditions in the country did not warrant active steps being taken; but after the Liberal government came into power in 1921 the Progressive group, as the minister will recall, was most insistent that action should be taken, and while no vote was taken in this house it will be found that in 1923 the government of the day declined to take any action towards completing the road. The reasons given were that the conditions did not warrant the expenditure at that time. Apparently at that moment the present Minister of Railways and Canals 'himself shared that view. In 1926 the present Minister of Finance became Minister of Railways, and at the session of 1926, this matter was discussed at considerable length. The discussion will be found in Hansard of June 8 and June 9, 1926. The then Minister of Railways was asking for a grant to rehabilitate the road, and at pages 4191 and 4192 of Hansard, he said:
I do not want to complicate this particular vote-[DOT]
That is the vote for rehabilitation:
-because there will be a discussion of that later, but I think probably it -would be as well to have all the information on Hansard.
It is estimated that it will cost $6,153,000 to complete the railway. It is estimated that the harbour works at Port Nelson, including elevator accommodation to the extent of 4,000,000 bushels-I would ask my hon. friend to bear in mind that that is not yet decided upon, but the estimate does include provision for it-with accommodation in the harbour for ten ships at the same time, will cost $20,200,000.
And on page 4192 Mr. Dunning said:
Now, in connection with these figures I want it distinctly understood that I am not commit-ing the government to this expenditure. I anticipated being asked a question as to what the engineering estimates were with respect to the completion of the terminal at Port Nelson. I want, in this connection, to revert to my

previous statement: It is the policy of the government to complete this route as economically as possible in order to enable a fair trial of it to be made. While I have carefully gone over the figure with respect to the vote which is now before the committee and have carefully gone over the figures with respect to the cost of completing the 92 miles of railway, I cannot say that it has been possible to do the same thing with reference to the estimated cost of the work at Nelson.
Then on page 4193 in reply to a question, Mr. Dunning said:
Now we understand each other. My point is that so far as the testing of the route is concerned it is something which has been a matter of repeated discussion and repeated investigation from a theoretical point of view, for the last forty years1.
There is further discussion of the cost for the completion of the terminals at Port Nelson, and in the end this is what was said by the then minister as reported at page 4194:
It must be quite apparent to my bon. friend that investigation is required before one can determine precisely the aids to navigation which are needed. Previous information on the subject does not lead me to believe that any considerable expenditure will be necessary in connection with lighthouses and things of that sort through the strait, and the bay is open sea. Provision is made in the estimates which I have just dealt with for a lighthouse at the entrance to Nelson channel. There are related questions upon which I could give general information in a little time. I thought there would be a more or less general discussion which would give me an opportunity of feeding the information more gradually than I have been able to do so far.
The discussion was somewhat lengthy having regard to what the minister said, that is, that he was not then undertaking to complete the 92 miles to the bay but to rehabilitate the existing railway which terminated, I think, at mileage 332, although a part of the roadbed was constructed beyond that point. That is, he asked only for a grant for rehabilitation and he made a statement to the house, as I have read, indicating what would be necessary to complete the railway and the terminals at Port Nelson. In that regard it is important also to observe that that very day he was asked whether or not there was any intention on the part of the government to shift the terminals from Port Nelson to any other point, and he replied that such was not the intention of the government at that time. So that in June, 1926, the government had seen no reason to change the proposed terminals from Port Nelson to Fort Churchill or else-where; and in the spring of 1926, after the government had been in power for some years, the undertaking had not been proceeded with beyond the effort made in June to secure

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
the necessary capital to rehabilitate the road as constructed to within 92 miles of the bay.
In succeeding years appropriations were granted by parliament to complete the road, but before the road was completed the minister, on the advice of Mr. Palmer, changed the terminus from Port Nelson to Fort Churchill. In that regard the Right Hon. Mr. Graham, the former Minister of Railways, in another chamber indicated that on the report of the engineers it was decided to make Nelson the terminal before his government went out of power in 1911, and that when Mr. Cochrane after a personal visit to Port Nelson and Fort Churchill concluded that the terminus should be at Port Nelson, he did so on the reports of the engineers of his department. That is common ground, both from the observations made by Mr. Graham in the Senate and from the statements made in this chamber by the then Minister of Railways and Canals, Mr. Cochrane. So that the terminus selected by both parties on the report of the engineers of the department was Port Nelson up to 1926, when the now Minister of Finance stated the government had no intention at the moment to change the terminus.
At a later date, in consequence of investigations made by the government, the terminals at Port Nelson were abandoned on the report of Mr. Palmer, and the work on terminals at Fort Churchill was commenced.
Now, it must be abundantly clear that there is nothing upon the records of this house to which any member can point that at any time there has been any inclination on m3r part or on the part of anyone else to do other than the very thing the government itself said it desired to do-to investigate before acting. It was in consequence of that very policy being pursued that the terminus was changed from Port Nelson to Fort Churchill, for had the minister proceeded without further investigation and carried out the declared policy of the government in 1926, the terminus would have been Port Nelson and not Fort Churchill. But because the minister desired in the light of the information he had received that further opportunity should be afforded for investigation, that investigation did take place and the terminus was changed to Fort Churchill, with the consequent abandonment of the terminals that had been constructed at Port Nelson. The expenditures on those terminals, as the minister pointed out last session, amounted to a very considerable sum, $6,000,000. Those expenditures had been made largely by the hon. gentleman's predecessors in office, acting under
the authority of this parliament, with money that had been appropriated for the purpose by the House of Commons and Senate of Canada.
Now, it is quite clear-let there be no misunderstanding about it-that the terminus at Port Nelson was selected, alike by Liberal and Conservative governments, on the recommendation of the engineers of the department.

That was reported in the press and amongst other papers in the Yorkton Enterprise of July 6, 1911, when Sir Robert Borden was making his tour through that section of the country. When the government of Sir Robert Borden met the house for the first time in November, 1911, the speech from the throne contained this paragraph:
The selection of the best route for the Hudson Bay railway is engaging the attention of my advisers, and an announcement will be made to you of the result of their inquiry.
I had the privilege of moving the adoption of the address in reply in the House of Commons on November 20, 1911, and in the course of my remarks I said:
It is, therefore, of vital importance in the minds and thoughts of those who produce grain in the west that no mistake be made so far as the terminals at Hudson Bay are concerned, and we rejoice that the speedy completion of the railway will be one of the matters which will receive the most earnest consideration of this administration. It is a matter in which the people in the west are vitally interested, that terminals shall be constructed there under the control of a commission, and that no private corporation will have an opportunity to unnecessarily control or dominate those terminals. That will obviate the necessity, of course, of our having to expropriate them, as we may some of the terminals at the head of the lakes.
I have already indicated the action taken by the administration of Sir Robert Borden, and the journey of Mr. Cochrane to that section of the country and the selection of the terminus for the railway. The war followed and operations were suspended, but it will be within the memory of this house, if it has followed what I have said, that the railway was completed to within 92 miles of Port Nelson and within 179 miles of Churchill when the present administration came into power. It will also be recalled that in 1926, when the present Minister of Finance was in control of the Department of Railways and Canals, further investigations were made which resulted in the terminals being changed from Port Nelson to Fort Churchill where the terminals mentioned by the Minister of Railways and Canals are now being constructed.
I think that makes the matter perfectly clear with one exception. Between 1911 and 1926 the Senate committee had investigated the whole question, and the answers I gave to the questions put to me in 1926 were made subsequent to that report. I do not now recall whether or not the Minister of Railways and Canals referred to the report in the course of 
his remarks, but all members interested in the Hudson Bay railway development will recall that that report was one of the factors, as the minister very properly said this morning, that brought about the further investigation as to whether Port Nelson should remain the terminus of the Hudson Bay line.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not wish to develop any controversy in reference to this matter except in regard to my hon. friend's remarks as to the sequence of events. His remarks have departed somewhat from my understanding of the sequence, and I shall be very brief in my reply. I think my hon. friend will agree that his last remarks regarding the length of time will call for some reply. Chronologically the position is stated approximately correctly by the leader of the opposition. The first sod was turned on the Hudson Bay railway in 1910, and work continued on it throughout the war period. In fact work was not stopped until a month or so before the close of the war. At the time of the cessation of work the railway had reached mile 332, some 90 miles from Nelson and 179 miles from Churchill. At that time it was the intention of the then government to build the road through to Nelson, but for a number of years after 1918 no work was done on the railway. Trains were operated once a month and sometimes not that often for a short distance along the line only. In 1926 as my hon. friend has stated I became Minister of Railways and in that session on behalf of the government I asked parliament for a vote of 83,000,000 for the rehabilitation of the existing railway. When asking for the vote I stated plainly that it would all be necessary to rebuild the line. My hon. friend has spoken of the 332 miles as if in 1926 it would have been possible to begin building the remaining portion. As a matter of fact in 1926 it was not possible for a train to get anywhere near the end of the existing steel because in the years which had intervened between 1918 and 1926 the road-bed which was built originally on muskeg had completely disappeared over large portions of the distance, particularly from mile 200 to mile 332. As a matter of actual fact so far as practical purposes are concerned it has been necessary to rebuild the whole of the former Hudson Bay railway in addition to constructing the remaining mileage to Churchill. With respect to the five years to which my hon. friend has referred I would like in the first place to place before him the actual facts. The date of the debate in this house was June 9, 1926, and on that date not one dollar was yet available with which to do anything. Shortly afterwards my hon. friends opposite came into office for a short time. I did not resume the position of Minister of Railways and Canals until some time in October of 1926. It is now the month of May, 1930, and at this point I wish to remind my hon. friend that September of 1926 is not five years distant. I think as a matter of fact he said it was six years.
No, I said it would be six years next year when it is completed.

Mr. Chairman, there is

Have a careful investigation made of all the circumstances-the nature of the port and the channel: the shifting character of the sand bars; the possibility of erecting proper docks; the availability of material for the construction of such docks: the cost of elevators; the time required in the movement of grain from Port Nelson to Liverpool; the dangers that would be encountered in transportation, so that the insurance rate might be determined; and other allied questions. Mr. Chairman, I would
like to direct the attention of the minister to a matter which I consider to be worthy of consideration. That portion of the Canadian National Railways, formerly the old National Transcontinental, running from the eastern boundary of Manitoba into the province of Quebec, is not subject to municipal and school taxation. The remainder of the Canadian National system pays full taxes, and I do not see why this other portion of the road should not be in the same position, especially with respect to the pioneer communities in northern Ontario. The towns of Sioux Lookout, Long-lac and Nakina are more particularly affected by this situation. I submit that it is unfair for the employees of the railway who live in these communities to have to pay municipal and school taxes which should be paid by the railway company. The employees of the railway in other communities receive the benefit of taxation paid by the company, and these people should be put in a like position. The town of Sioux Lookout, an important divisional point, offers a concrete illustration. The assessments in that community, outside of railway property, amount to something like $900,000, while the assessment on the railway property amounts to a little over $430,000. It will be seen that over one-third of the assessed value of the community belongs to the railway, and yet no taxation is paid. That condition should be remedied. This is a community of some 1,750 people comprising perhaps 500 families, and each family is forced to pay at least $50 to S60 more per year because the railway is not taxed. The assessments in Nakina in 1924 amounted to $96,000, while for this year they should amount to $120,000. Nearly one-half of the taxes paid in that community should be paid by the railway company. These same facts would apply to the towns of Hudson, Allanwater and Armstrong, but let us consider the case of Long-lac. In this community a certain portion of the railway property is taxed while another portion is not. This is a very anomalous situation. It is estimated by these communities, and particularly by Sioux Lookout that the railway owes them over $200,000 in back taxes. That is a considerable burden upon the people of that community. This government has had

Mr. C-OTNAM: I would like to direct the attention of the minister to the question of seniority of certain conductors and brakemen formerly employed on the Ottawa division of the former Grand Trunk railway. Perhaps the best method of doing this would be to read a letter which I have received covering this point. It is as follows:
When the amalgamation of the Grand Trunk and the Canadian Northern took place all the freight traffic was diverted away from the Ottawa division and a number of our men were thrown out of employment. New men were engaged on other divisions while men on the Ottawa division were without work.
We have been looking to the Brotherhood of Railway trainmen for the past six or seven years to effect a settlement whereby we would be given work according to our seniority. A settlement was put into effect April 1, this year (they could not have chosen a better date to put it into effect as we were worse off than ever). The engineers and firemen of the Ottawa division received a settlement. They were given their seniority and a larger territory to work on, also the agents and operators were given their seniority on a larger territory, maintenance of way men, water service men, shopmen and carmen have all been given consideration while we have been left to the Ottawa division with practically nothing to do.
We used to have as high as fifty crews in extra service comprising one hundred and fifty men, to-day we have only about four crews. As seniority is the foundation of all labour organizations and all other men affected have received their seniority we cannot understand why we cannot get the same. Yard brakemen who belong to our organization received their seniority; where there were two separate terminals they were joined into one.
The present settlement was made by the representatives of the men and our delegate accepted it. It turns out now that a lot of things went on he did not know about and we are going to have to suffer for his mistakes. The men of the former Ottawa division have protested this in a body to our labour union. Other districts which have profited by the amalgamation naturally want things to remain as they are and as they are in the majority they control the vote at our meetings. As it stands now men on this division with fifteen to twenty years seniority are without^ work and men with ten years seniority working on other divisions are employed. We consider this unfair and would like you to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Labour or Minister of Railways and could take up with the President of the Canadian National with a view of giving us justice. We have been patiently waiting for years for our organization to effect a settlement but their settlement is far from being any assistance to us. I am sure all men affected would be agreeable to a board of arbitration composed of railwaymen who would be neutral to all parties affected.
In view of the statements contained in that letter, I should like to ask the minister whether he will give me an assurance that this matter of seniority for these men will be taken uip with the president of the Canadian National Railways and adjusted at as early a date as possible.

The matter is primarily

I shall be glad to draw it to the attention of the management of the railways, but I do not care to give my hon. friend any assurance that I will intrude myself into the management of the railways to tell them what they should do in this or any other matter of management.

Just a word in support of
the representations of my good friend the hon. member for Jacques Cartier. We represent contiguous constituencies, both of which suffer very keenly on account of the fact that the canal separates one part of the population of Montreal from another. As hon. members are aware, Montreal is a place of some importance. This means practically every ten minutes during the day while navigation lasts. We see frequently several street cars, sometimes eight, ten or twelve, lined up waiting for the bridges to open and people going to business suffer acutely on account of the obstruction of the traffic. I can understand that the minister did not care to have the supplementary estimates appear too large, but we want to have some assurance that the government is going to come to our aid. We are in absolute need of this improvement j it must tske place. We are suffering on account of a canal which is a government institution. If the subways were built, it would of course facilitate the passenger traffic to and from the city of Verdun, and would also greatly facilitate the passage of boats through the canal. I think I can say to my hon. friends who have made this request that the department will be prepared to make a contribution of $1,000,000, or at any rate I will say that I would be prepared to recommend such a contribution purely on the basis of its being a businesslike construction, as soon as the city of Montreal and the Montreal Tramways Company come to an agreement as to the amount which they will contribute to the building of these subways.
Has the minister ever heard of the Oshawa railway station?

That makes it worse.

Let my hon. friend possess his soul in patience until I have made my explanation. But the item was not put in the estimates because it is not required until the other parties reach an agreement. When they do,
I am prepared to recommend that an amount equal to $1,000,000 be provided through the estimates of the Railway department on the ground that this is a business arrangement which will improve the service on the canal and improve the service to the residents of Verdun, and will not mean any additional cost to the government of Canada.

The men engaged on the ship canals have been working eleven and thirteen hours a day, and sometimes a twenty-four hour shift. Mr, SIMPSON: Will that apply to the canal at the Soo where the traffic is practically continuous?

I cannot answer my hon. friend as to that at the moment. It will apply at the Soo if the conditions warrant. I do not know the amount of traffic passing through the Canadian Soo; my impression is the great bulk of it passes through the American Soo.

While that is true, it is accounted for by the fact that there are four locks on the American side and only one on our side. But notwithstanding that, quite a substantial portion of the traffic passes through on the Canadian side of the river. For years these men have been working long hours, while just across the river the men have been on the eight-hour shift for several years and are getting more money than our men. If any change is being made on the canal system,
I appeal to the minister to take care of the men at the Soo.
I shall be very glad to take it into consideration, and if the facts warrant the eight-hour day being applied, I will see that it is applied.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: The expenditures have been practically for the same sort of services for which votes have been asked for several years past. One of the recommendations made at that time was that the army pay corps as a separate unit should be gradually dispensed with in view of the suggested changes in the accounting branch and the appointment of district accountants. If time permitted I should like to go fully into that, but perfMr. Ralston.]
haps I can indicate the general idea to the committee. It is that in the department, as far as the officers who are now administering it are concerned, the intention is as far as possible to utilize civilian services more generally but to use of course military services when the technical nature of the employment requires it, or in other words not to build up a large military establishment in collateral services. The situation which existed and which I may say still' exists is that the army pay corps and the accounting branch duplicate their work to some extent. The accountants branch has to keep the accounts of the department generally. The pay corps keeps certain accounts in connection with certain essentially military services which also have to be included in the accountant's books as well. The information for the pay corps in many instances has to come from the chief accountant's branch to the pay corps-for instance accounts for general supply. There seemed no reason to Mr. Gordon Scott for having these two sets of accounts.
The pay corps as we generally think of it is for the purpose of paying the troops, but in this instance they are keeping a lot of other accounts, as well. It was felt, however, that accounting was principally a civilian occupation, and not only Mr. Scott but my departmental advisers concurred in the recommendation. As yet no change in personnel has been made, but an instruction was issued that from March 1 the pay corps should come under the chief accountant's branch, and that is the situation at the present time. The idea expressed in the instruction from the adjutant general was that there should be as little as possible individual hardship worked on the members of the pay corps, and that the personnel as far as their qualifications permitted and vacancies exist would be absorbed in the civil organization. At present the only change which has been made is the transfer of the administration of the pay corps from the adjutant general to the chief accountant, looking forward to the time when it may be absorbed in the accounting branch. Naturally I am concerned with the dislocation which any administration change like this causes and I want to have it seen to that the dislocation be just as slight as possible.

After all this is the
Department of National Defence, and one would naturally expect that as far as possible the developments should take place along military lines. From what the minister says,
I understand it is proposed to transfer the military pay portion of the service to the civilian pay force. To me this is regrettable.
I quite understand that there may be dupli-

cations; I understand that it is desirable to improve the organization and administration, but I should have thought the pay branch would have been kept under the militia services and not put under a civilian branch. These different departmental corps aid in the efficiency of the department. Surely the minister does not suggest that civilian employees, without necessarily any military training, are as efficient as the permanently trained pay corps? That applies to the other branches of departmental corps. They are there for the purpose of efficiency and for training, and in the event of the forces requiring to take the field what would the minister do? He would be employing civilians.
We would do exactly what we did in the last war; during the last war the civilians enlisted and went into uniform.

They still had to go
through a process of training.

Not so much for the
accountants.

I submit that the pay
branch of an army, especially in the field, carries on a very important and complicated duty. Civilians are not enlisted men.

Perhaps my hon. friend
does not understand the situation in the British army. I think probably during the war the Canadians were one of the few forces who had battalion paymasters; in the British army they had what they called field cashiers, civilians I understand, who came with the cash to a certain point, carrying the pay for perhaps a division, and who distributed the cash to the battalion commanders, who in turn distributed it to the company commanders, who, under the old British system as at present, as my hon. friend knows, paid their men. The company commander was supposed to be the father of his men, and if a man had a complaint about his pay or allowances, the pay parade when he came before his company commander was the time to make that complaint known. I should think if we ever have the misfortune to go into the field again that system might have a good deal to commend it as compared to the practice of having regimental paymasters such as we had in the last war. That is just an opinion. I mention the system to my hon. friend to remind him that it has been recognized elsewhere that the fact that a man happens to be in uniform does not necessarily equip him any better for cashier's work.
But the man in uniform could do it with equal efficiency.
But not because he is in uniform.

Surely the minister does not mean to say that civilians should go into the field, not being under discipline and not being enlisted like any other officer, and that these men would be just as efficient?

My hon. friend is talking about a permanent pay corps. I see nothing especially advantageous in the system we had in the last war of having regimental paymasters. I think the company commander might be a better and more logical paymaster.

Surely the minister does not suggest that the commanding officer should be responsible for the pay. We tried that out in the smaller units and it was an absolute failure. Whoever handles the cash should be under discipline, and should not be a civilian.

But the paymaster was a
battalion officer; he was not on the pay corps. Now I should like to ask a question. As I understand it the training vote this year is about 825,000 more than it was last year for the non-permanent active militia?
No, it is just the same.

Then are we training fewer
men?

No, I think not. It is
exactly the same amount this year.

I am sorry I must bring up a matter now which may delay the committee for a few minutes, but I do not believe I can afford to let it go. I refer to a matter which I think is known to a number of members and to many officials in the department. In July last tenders were called for the supply of coal in Kingston. These tenders were received on July 19. There were three tenders for this coal in the city of Kingston, but on July 25 another tender was received from one of the companies and on July 29 a third tender was received. The result was that this tenderer was able to reduce his first figure of S12.22 to 812.12. No such opportunity was given to the other tenderers, and although the company which sent in the three tenders reduced the price by 2 cents and in another case by 10 cents, at the same time the company was enabled to raise the price on one quality of coal in order to make up for what was lost on the
Supply-National Defence

other two tenders. I submit, shortly, that this is a most unfair system; if a second and third tender is to be allowed in respect to these supplies, then every person who made a tender in the first place should be given the same privilege. There are certain regulations governing the weighing of the coal. When this firm had been permitted to submit the second and third tenders they should have been satisfied, but I find from the records of the department that this coal was not weighed on military scales. The payments have been made, the coal is in the bins, and we must let it go.
A third method of delivery was by truck. Weights were submitted for 8,800 pounds 8,700 pounds and 8,400 pounds, but it was finally discovered that the scales upon which this coal had been weighed had a capacity of only 8,000 pounds. It is to the credit of some official of the department that this discrepancy was discovered, and a certain amount of money was refunded. If that were done with a few truckloads, how much did the department suffer in the delivery of 1,500 cartloads which came in unweighed?
These tenders have been handled in a very unfair manner. I find that the department has two kinds of notices. One is sent to the tenderer when he is not the lowest; if he is the lowest and does not get the contract, he receives a different kind of notice. That is a most unusual method to be adopted by any department, and one which enables people to bid the second time. This matter should be investigated and had I known of it earlier I would have brought it before the house earlier in the session.

When my hon. friend mentioned the other day the matter of the return, I made inquiry of the deputy just before he went away and I understood that the difficulty was as to the weigh bills. As my hon. friend knows, I arranged that he should be allowed to see the original weigh bills.

I took advantage of that opportunity and it was from that examination that I discovered that the regulations had never been complied with. It was claimed that they possessed two or three signatures of the quartermaster, but there was not a single item of payment which was initialled by that gentleman. I might state that the man who was supposed to weigh this coal was taken away on the last day by the tenderer. There should have been a check made of the weigh bills presented by the tenderer, and military form No. 19 should have been used. However, that was not done in the case of about 1,100 cartloads.

I thought the only matter in dispute was with regard to the weigh bills, and I asked the department and the commandant to give me a report in this regard. Therefore I ?.n unable to give my hon. friend all the facts which he desired. Two tenders were put in-
There were three.

My officer here tells me that two tenders at least were put in for delivery at two different places. One tenderer quoted a different price for each place and the other tenderer quoted a flat rate. Later on, without any suggestion either directly or indirectly from the department, a telegram was received from the tenderer who had quoted different prices for each delivery point quoting the lower price for both delivery points. This telegram was received before the time for receiving tenders had elapsed and the contract was awarded to that particular tenderer.
The report of the commandant regarding the weighing of the coal is as follows:
It is explained that, although M.F.B. 19 has not been utilized, nevertheless all of the coal was weighed on the government weigh scales at Kingston by a qualified representative of the commandant, R.M.C. in the person of E. H. West, caretaker, R.M.C., whose signature is appended to weigh bills, with the exception of those signed by the quartermaster himself. The other signature, viz., that of A. Cockerham, cleaner and helper, R.M.C., vouches for the actual receipt of each load of coal at the R.M.C. at the end of the journey between the government weigh scale in the city of Kingston and the R.M.C. grounds. The greatest possible supervision and care has been exercised over the weighing and cartage of this coal; the government weigh scale was daily visited by the quartermaster R.M.C. who personally witnessed during his visits the weighing of coal and has himself signed certain weigh bills, in addition to giving his certificate on the fact of the firm's account.
So long as the coal was weighed on government weigh scales and the weighing carried out -as has been done in this case-by a responsible and competent civil employee representing the R.M.C., it was felt that the regulations governing the receipt of coal were being properly and adequately carried out; importance was unfortunately not attached to the use of M.F.B. 19 to record weights, in fact the regulation governing this point did not come to mind when the forms supplied by contractor were taken into use. As soon, however, as it was pointed out by district auditor that M.F.B. 19 should he used, a supply of that form was immediately obtained from the D.S. and T.O.. M.D. No. 3. and is now being utilized, and will accompany the accounts for the balance of the coal still clue under this contract.
That is signed by C. F. Constantine, Brigadier, commandant, Royal Military College.
